#67437. How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that people often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan.
  • I like to create purpose-driven designs.
  • Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that people often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a new house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

It has been revealed that the same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

In a latest garden, the major goal is often screening. Most people want privacy to live their lives outside without having to see a neighboring house, road, commercial area, or vacant lot.

Privacy was one of the major considerations when planning my grass garden. There was no privacy between my property and the neighboring property. I could see my neighbors eat their dinner, watch them play with their grandchildren, and even see them argue. Their house was also too close to the property line, and in fact, their sidewalk was on my property. That was a problem.

Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

I started out with some tall elements at the back of the bed to start the screening process. I positioned these plants so I could maintain them from my property without having branches extend over the property line. Keeping their mature size in mind also helped avoid potential conflicts with the neighboring property. Soft screens made of trees and tall shrubs (both evergreen and deciduous) offer privacy without creating a harsh, artificial boundary line.

Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options.

Looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

In a recent development, understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

What a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden.

Growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from big cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

Even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build new nests.

The ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

Discuss this article or ask gardening questions with a regional gardening expert on the Gardening Answers forum.

And for more Pacific Northwest regional reports, click here.

Susan Calhoun is the owner and principal designer of Plantswoman Design in Bainbridge Island, Washington.

Arianne and Micah’s Small Urban Minneapolis Garden

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD.
  • Today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota.
  • In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hi GPOD! I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD. Unfortunately, I haven’t received any submissions through the form in quite a while. I’m not sure what the problem is, but hopefully there will be a resolution soon. In the meantime, you can submit your photos and captions through the email linked below instead.

Today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:.

In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

Sources indicate that arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

Absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

Sources indicate that one of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

There is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

Industry observers note that just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

Another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

Tall conifers create a fantastic privacy screen in this view. The garden really is its own secluded paradise.

A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

Sources indicate that zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

Thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something fresh to admire.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy.
  • This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.
  • My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

According to recent reports, this is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

It has been revealed that in the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

In a recent development, sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy claims she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what new plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to the Fine Homebuilding Podcast, our weekly discussion of building, remodeling, and design topics aimed at anybody who cares deeply about the craft and science of working on houses.
  • In a recent development, please email us your questions to [email protected].
  • Patrick: Upcoming article about surge protection by Chad McClung.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to the Fine Homebuilding Podcast, our weekly discussion of building, remodeling, and design topics aimed at anybody who cares deeply about the craft and science of working on houses. This is senior editor Patrick McCombe. I’m joined by Green Building Advisor editor Randy Williams, Fine Homebuilding contributing editor and operations manager for TDS Design/Build in Madison, Wisconsin, and producer Cari Delahanty.

In a recent development, please email us your questions to [email protected]. You can find previous podcasts and check out the show notes at finehomebuilding.com/podcast.

Ian: House painting, interesting TDS projects.

Randy: Green Building Advisor updates.

Patrick: Upcoming article about surge protection by Chad McClung.

In a recent development, grant referred to a house where he recently stayed as a “tiny house,” describing it as being about 16 ft. x 30 ft. I guess I have lived in a “tiny house” for 20 years! Ours is a Cape, built in 1953 by the people from whom we bought it. It has a 24-ft. x 26-ft. footprint and no dormer.

As discussed on the podcast, there are a lot of great things about a house this size. However, it is, in fact, too small. It is too small to comfortably fit furniture or closets or a family to gather to watch a movie. Our “primary bedroom” is 10 ft. x 11 ft. with a small closet out of that boundary.

According to recent reports, the full house could be arranged to be a very nice size for a couple, but it feels too small for four of us, especially with only one bathroom. I’m not sure how we’ve worked out the lack of closet space and single bathroom with three women plus me, but we have. When my daughters were in high school, I found it emotionally uncomfortable that most of their friends had bigger and nicer homes.

Sources indicate that putting my hurt ego aside, I feel they are lucky to be able to appreciate future living spaces that will likely be more luxurious than they are used to. My oldest daughter definitely had a better bedroom at college and easier access to a bathroom!

Discussion of Chris Briley’s recent low-voltage lighting article on Green Building Advisor.

This article, “Low Voltage Lighting,” is from Chris’ Pretty Good House blog. Chris suggests that given the low energy consumption of LED lighting, do we still need line voltage lighting circuits anymore? Randy, can you briefly explain Chris’s premise? What do you think as an electrician? Does it make sense to switch our wiring methods for modern lighting? Ian, what do you think about this?

When you look at a finished house, what are the small details that make you feel the builder really took the time to do things right?

Industry observers note that I’m not talking about expensive finishes or high-end appliances. I’m thinking more about the little things that might not stand out in photos but make a difference once you actually live in the house—clean trim work, well-planned storage, good lighting, quiet doors, sensible outlets, properly finished transitions, etc.

I’ve noticed that some of the most enjoyable spaces aren’t necessarily the most expensive ones. They just seem to have fewer little annoyances because someone thought through how the space would actually be used.

It has been revealed that for those of you who have built or remodeled homes, what is one relatively small detail you’re especially glad you included? And is there anything you wish you’d thought about before construction was finished?

I’m curious whether the things people appreciate most are usually visible design choices or the less noticeable details behind the walls and throughout the house.

We talked about what gives you confidence in a builder, so now let’s talk about what you see most often on construction sites that is done poorly or incorrectly?

Hi GPOD! Yesterday we enjoyed some beautiful fall color in Nancy’s Massachusetts garden, and today we’re heading west to see what fall looked like in Colorado this year.

Sources indicate that bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie claims the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:.

Colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

Welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

Other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

Another view from the front yard.

A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

Thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

The Best Cordless Drills for Home Repairs and Heavy-Duty Projects

Industry observers note that cordless drills make it easier to bore holes and drive screws without a cord restricting movement. Among the most useful battery-powered tools, they serve everyone from occasional DIYers to busy renovation pros. To find the best cordless drills for different projects, we tested 14 highly rated models, from heavy-duty hammer drills to compact drill/drivers.

Recent findings suggest that choosing a quality drill means finding the right balance of power, control, and comfort for the work ahead. We evaluated cordless electric drills for quality, torque, ease of use, and power, testing each function to identify where every model excelled. Our top recommendation is the Bosch GSB18V-65B12 18-volt ½-inch hammer drill driver, which is well-balanced, highly maneuverable, and offers great cost value.

It has been revealed that whether you need extra muscle for demanding work or a smaller tool for crafting and household repairs, a good cordless drill should suit your projects and budget. Our tested picks cover a range of needs.

Industry observers note that the following cordless drills represent many of the drill brands known for reliability and value, and we tested each one. We tested each tool to determine its power, durability, battery life, and overall quality. For shoppers comparing DeWalt vs. Milwaukee, the battery platform and available tools are also worth considering.

The Bosch GSB18V-65B12 earned our Best Overall cordless drill award for its compact build and outstanding performance across a wide range of drilling and driving tasks. This lightweight cordless drill proved comfortable for extended daily use and powerful enough for occasional heavy-duty work. The kit includes the drill with a pre-installed belt hook, a 2.0 amp-hour battery, charger, and tool bag.

This pro-quality model was smaller and lighter than the other 18-volt drills we tested, making it easier to maneuver in confined workspaces. Pound for pound, it was stronger, too. Its 575 inch-pounds of maximum torque handled hardened steel, concrete, and brick without binding and drove heavy-duty construction screws and lag bolts with ease.

Even in concrete and brick, we found hammer mode unnecessary: Low speed and firm downward pressure were enough. However, when the bit reached about an inch deep, its straight shank began slipping in the chuck. Retightening allowed us to finish the hole, but slippage occurred three times during testing. The drill had ample power, but three-flat-shank bits may provide a more secure grip.

Sources indicate that what our tester says: “I really liked how the newly introduced Bosch hammer drill/driver felt—light, comfortable, and capable. In terms of comfort, as well as speed and torque, I preferred it over all of the other drills that I tested.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer.

Get the Bosch 18V cordless drill at Amazon or Acme Tools.

The Black+Decker 20V MAX PowerConnect brushless drill/driver combines affordability with useful power and features for home projects. For buyers seeking a cordless drill with battery and charger, this kit includes both, along with a double-ended screwdriver bit and belt clip. The 2.0 amp-hour battery also works with other compatible Black+Decker PowerConnect tools.

The brushless motor delivers up to 486 inch-pounds of torque, while the ½-inch keyless metal chuck accepts larger-shank bits than the ⅜-inch chucks on some entry-level drills. Two speed ranges—0 to 450 and 0 to 1,900 RPM—cover screwdriving and drilling tasks. We found the ten clutch settings prevented overdriving fasteners when assembling furniture or installing hardware, and a separate drilling position provides access to full power.

We like its compact body, soft-grip handle, and built-in LED—they make the drill a good option for working inside cabinets and other confined spaces. The magnetic bit holder keeps a spare bit within reach, while the battery indicator displays remaining charge. Starting screws may require a light touch on the variable-speed trigger, so the lower gear is useful for more controlled driving. The single included battery suits intermittent household projects, though a spare would help keep longer work sessions moving.

Get the Black+Decker cordless drill at Amazon, Lowe’s, or Black+Decker.

According to recent reports, the DeWalt DCD1007WW1 is a heavy-duty drill with an efficient brushless motor that produces up to 1,530 watts. Although it was among the more expensive drills we tested, its rugged construction and heavy-duty performance help justify the investment. The kit includes a ½-inch three-speed hammer drill, removable side handle, belt hook, 8-amp-hour battery, charger, and tool bag.

In a recent development, we pushed this drill harder during testing, and it delivered. It drilled ½-inch holes in wood faster than any other model we tested, with similarly strong results in steel, brick, and concrete. It also drove every ½-inch lag bolt flush without a pilot hole, then finished driving bolts another drill had left halfway in. After these initial tests, the battery indicator still revealed a full charge. DeWalt claims up to 275 holes per charge.

This cordless hammer drill was also surprisingly maneuverable thanks to its short motor-and-chuck assembly. Although slightly heavier than the older DeWalt DCD996 we compared it with, it was about an inch shorter. That compact shape helped it fit tighter spaces and feel more balanced when working at different angles. Still, at roughly twice the weight of many 18-volt drills, it is best suited to demanding projects that warrant the extra power.

Another useful feature is the adjustable LED at the base of the handle. Unlike lights that operate only with the trigger, this one pivots to three positions and can stay on independently for up to 20 minutes. It is brighter than a smartphone flashlight and offers a practical alternative to putting a phone within reach of a dimly lit repair.

It has been revealed that what our tester indicates: “The DeWalt 20-volt hammer drill felt like it could do anything, and the shorter nose allowed it to do quite a bit more than its predecessors. It’s incredibly powerful for a cordless drill, and it held a super strong grip on the bit shaft.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer.

Get the DeWalt cordless drill at Lowe’s, The Home Depot, or Acme Tools.

Industry observers note that the standout feature of the Makita 7.2V cordless driver-drill is its hinged body, which converts from a pistol grip to an in-line configuration like an electric screwdriver. We were especially interested in how the straight grip would improve access when using this small cordless drill.

We began testing with a fully charged battery, the pistol grip, and a small hex-shank paddle bit. The chuck doesn’t accept round-shank bits, which limits bit compatibility. As expected, this 7.2V model lacked the power of the larger drills we tested, but it isn’t intended to compete with a professional 20V drill. It’s designed primarily for drilling wood and drywall, and it handled those tasks well.

The in-line grip proved most useful when installing fasteners in tight spaces, such as cabinet slides and hinges. In that configuration, the Makita worked like a cordless screwdriver with extra power. Its 21-setting clutch let us adjust the torque to suit different fasteners before disengaging, while two speed settings added versatility.

Industry observers note that if we could keep only one drill/driver for everyday household tasks, we’d choose this Makita. It isn’t a construction drill, but its ability to reach awkwardly positioned fasteners makes it especially useful around the house. It ran for nearly 30 minutes before the battery needed recharging. The LED illuminated the work area and flashed to alert us when the charge ran low.

Get the Makita DF012DSE cordless drill at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Acme Tools.

In a recent development, the Ryobi PCL206K2 carries on the brand’s reputation for affordable, dependable tools. This 18V cordless drill has a ½-inch chuck, a maximum speed of 1,750 RPM, and 515 inch-pounds of torque, offering specifications comparable to many higher-priced models while weighing slightly more than 2.5 pounds. The kit includes two 1.5 amp-hour batteries and a charger.

In testing, the Ryobi delivered impressive drilling and driving speed and power. It bored effortlessly through a 2×4 with a ⅛-inch twist bit, then made a clean, precise hole with a spade bit in just 4 seconds. It was equally quick and effective at driving 3-inch deck screws. Performance nearly matched that of similarly sized brushless drills. We suspect its brushed motor would drain batteries faster, but it held its own in our drilling and driving tests.

The brushed motor and plastic chuck help explain the lower price. Professional-grade models typically use brushless motors and all-metal chucks for better battery life and durability. For weekend DIYers, though, this standard ½-inch drill delivers ample power and speed at an excellent value.

Get the Ryobi cordless drill at The Home Depot.

The Milwaukee M12 right-angle drill combines useful power with easy access to tight spaces. We tested the kit version, which includes a battery and charger, but those who already own Milwaukee M12 tools can purchase the tool-only model and use their existing batteries.

Sources indicate that weighing just 2.03 pounds, this compact drill slipped easily into confined spaces and was comfortable to operate with one hand. It lacked the power of some larger models we tested, making it better suited to furniture assembly and drilling small holes than heavy construction work. The built-in LED helped illuminate the work area, although we needed an additional work light in darker spots.

A welcome feature was the clutch, which helps prevent stripping screw heads when driving fasteners. The elongated trigger also let us shift our grip higher or lower on the handle without losing easy access to the control. For electricians, HVAC technicians, and plumbers who need controlled screwdriving or small-hole drilling in tight spaces, this Milwaukee is a useful option.

Get the Milwaukee right-angle drill at Amazon (tool only), Ace Hardware (tool only), or The Home Depot.

Sources indicate that small but mighty, this Bosch cordless drill came with several quick-change attachments that allowed us to drill holes and insert screws in various settings. We quickly discovered why this Bosch drill features what the manufacturer calls the FlexiClick system: The attachments connect via a simple push-and-click movement that locks them firmly in place. The drill has a standard attachment with a ⅜-inch chuck that accepts most drill and screw bits. It also has an offset attachment that allowed us to adjust the position of the bit to fit in hard-to-reach spots and an angle attachment that gives the Bosch drill a multiposition head for drilling at various slants.

According to recent reports, while this is just a 12-volt model, we found it had ample power and torque to drill holes in dimensional lumber using even a paddle bit. We also found the 20-position clutch helpful for adjusting the torque to keep from stripping out screw heads in both hardwood and softwood.

The LED guide light isn’t as bright as it could be—it may help slightly, but you will probably want to use a supplemental work light if you’re drilling in low-light situations. The belt clip on this tool is located at the back of the head, which we liked better than the drills with clips located at the base of the handle. It was easier to slip on and off our tool belts. This little drill won’t replace a full-power drill/driver, but it’s an excellent pick for tackling tasks in tight spots.

Get the Bosch 12V cordless drill at Amazon, Ace Hardware, or Acme Tools.

We spent 27 hours testing 14 highly rated cordless drills, drilling more than 500 holes and installing 200 screws and bolts. We evaluated drilling speed and power in materials such as wood, steel, brick, and concrete, along with screwdriving control and the ability to seat larger fasteners. We also assessed chuck security, grip comfort, weight, maneuverability in confined spaces, and the usefulness of features such as work lights, speed controls, and adjustable clutches.

Recent findings suggest that features such as battery performance and included accessories also informed our value assessments. Each drill received scores from 0 (lowest) to 5 (highest) for build quality, ease of use, performance, and value. We then compared cumulative scores within each voltage range and selected the strongest performers for different owners and project types.

It has been revealed that when choosing from different types of drills, start by matching their features to the needs of your projects. The most powerful cordless drill isn’t necessarily the best fit for occasional repairs, especially if its weight makes it tiring to use. As with all the best cordless tools, the ideal tool for the job tends to balance versatility, comfort, and value. Understanding how to use a drill also helps users get the most out of whatever drill you choose.

Battery voltage helps indicate a cordless drill’s capabilities, but it doesn’t measure power on its own. Motor design, gearing, and battery performance also matter. When choosing a battery-powered drill, consider the work you initiative to tackle rather than voltage alone.

The distinction between 18V and 20V MAX can be confusing. These labels describe the same voltage class: 20V is the maximum initial battery voltage measured without a workload, while 18V is the nominal voltage. The difference isn’t a startup surge, nor does a 20V MAX label guarantee more power than an 18V model. Similarly, many drills marketed as 12V use batteries rated at 10.8V nominal.

Use these categories as a starting point:.

For masonry projects, knowing how to drill into concrete will help you select the appropriate tool, bit, and technique.

In a recent development, battery capacity, measured in amp-hours (Ah), also matters. At the same voltage, a higher Ah rating generally means longer runtime, though actual results depend on the drill and workload. Smaller packs keep the tool lighter, while larger packs support longer work sessions but usually add weight and cost. A higher Ah rating alone doesn’t guarantee more drilling power. For occasional projects, a compact battery may be sufficient; for extended use, consider a larger pack or a spare.

Torque is the twisting force a drill delivers, while speed, measured in revolutions per minute (RPM), describes how rapidly the bit turns. A lower gear generally provides more torque for driving fasteners and drilling with larger bits. Higher speeds suit many smaller-bit drilling tasks, though the appropriate speed depends on the material and bit.

Most drills have an adjustable clutch that limits the torque transmitted to the chuck. When resistance reaches the selected setting, the clutch disengages to help prevent overdriving screws or stripping their heads. It responds to resistance rather than a preset screw depth, so choosing the right setting helps maintain control. Knowing how to change a drill bit also helps ensure the bit is properly seated and secured.

According to recent reports, look for at least 10 clutch settings to accommodate different fasteners and materials. A drilling machine with two gear settings offers more versatility, while a variable-speed trigger lets you fine-tune speed within the selected range.

It has been revealed that A drill’s size and weight affect comfort, especially during extended use. Lightweight models can weigh about a pound, while heavy-duty cordless hammer drills may exceed 8 pounds. Extra power often adds weight, so choose a tool that balances capability with comfortable handling. Check whether the listed weight includes the battery, which can make a noticeable difference.

A compact drill is easier to maneuver in confined spaces, and a smaller body doesn’t necessarily mean less power. Consider both weight and overall dimensions when comparing models.

According to recent reports, most cordless drills have keyless chucks for quick bit changes. Chuck capacity determines the largest bit-shank diameter the tool accepts, rather than the size of hole it can drill. Many general-purpose models have ⅜- or ½-inch chucks, while some compact drill/drivers use ¼-inch hex holders that accept only compatible hex-shank bits.

The best drill bits for a project must suit both the material and the drill’s chuck. Check compatibility before buying a bit set.

Sources indicate that corded drills sometimes come with a brushed motor. They are cheap and reliable, but the brushes eventually wear down and require replacement. Another challenge with brushed motors is that they create friction, which drains the battery faster in cordless models.

According to recent reports, the best cordless power drills often use a brushless motor. These virtually maintenance-free motors use the battery much more efficiently. However, brushless motors cost more. As a result, many budget cordless drills still use brushed motors.

For a typical DIYer, the difference is probably negligible. Those who want to maximize performance and runtime, particularly professional users, often choose a brushless cordless drill.

Like most modern battery-operated drills, the models in this guide use rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. Runtime depends on battery capacity and workload, while charging time varies with the battery and charger. For extensive drilling, a kit with a spare battery lets you keep working while the depleted pack charges.

Industry observers note that note that manufacturer runtime claims often factor backup batteries into their runtime estimates. For instance, the specs on a drill that comes with two batteries, each lasting 1 hour, may list a 2-hour runtime.

Additionally, many cordless drills include a smart charger that replenishes the battery faster, usually within 15 to 60 minutes. A charge indicator allows you to monitor battery capacity.

Depending on your projects, these extras can improve comfort and convenience:.

Industry observers note that A refurbished cordless drill can help you save money or afford a higher-quality model while reducing waste. Unlike ordinary secondhand tools, refurbished models usually undergo inspection, repairs, and testing before resale. Standards vary by seller, however, so check what “refurbished,” “reconditioned,” or “renewed” means for the listing.

These tools may come from customer returns or have sustained shipping or warehouse damage. Don’t assume they were barely used or restored to like-new condition. You can browse refurbished drills at Amazon.

Walmart and other retailers also offer refurbished options. Keep these considerations in mind:.

According to recent reports, buy from a reputable source and inspect and test the drill promptly after delivery. If something is wrong, you’ll have time to request a return.

Our in-depth investigation of technologies and specifications above may have you feeling better equipped to choose the best power drill for your needs. That valuable information is underlined by examples of some of the top cordless drills right now available. Still, with so many options available, a few questions might remain. The following are answers to some of the most common questions.

According to recent reports, the primary use of a cordless drill is for drilling holes and driving screws. However, you can also get numerous attachments, which are sometimes included in cordless drill sets. Stirrers, for example, can mix paint and other liquids. You can also attach a sanding drum, a wire brush for rust removal, or a polishing bonnet. Our guide covers more uses for your cordless drill/driver.

Corded models were once more powerful tools. But today, equally powerful cordless models rival them. However, cordless models lose some of their power over the course of the charge, while corded models perform at a consistent level for as long as they’re plugged in.

An electric screwdriver is usually much smaller, has less power, and cannot drill holes. The cordless drill can drill holes and also drive screws.

New and improved models enter the market all the time, so it’s difficult to name one brand as the best overall. Bosch, DeWalt, Makita, and Milwaukee all offer tools for different needs and budgets. Comparing individual models—including the best DeWalt drills—is more useful than choosing by brand alone.

Industry observers note that it very much depends on the amp hours of the battery and how hard the drill is working. A battery can last as little as 15 minutes, though many will run between 30 minutes and 1 hour. Buying a spare battery for your rechargeable drill lets you swap it out and keep working while the other charges.

Brushless electric motors are more efficient and powerful than brushed motors. They often last longer, too. But higher performance also comes at a higher price. For occasional light-duty drilling, brushed cordless drills are more cost-effective.

Sources indicate that the best voltage depends on the user’s needs. For instance, 12-volt drills are inexpensive and perfectly capable of light-duty drilling and driving, while 18-volt drills deliver the higher torque and faster RPM needed for medium- and heavy-duty projects.

Glenda Taylor is a product tester and writer specializing in construction, remodeling, and real estate. She tests a wide range of power tools as well as other home improvement, household, and lawn-and-garden products.

Mark Wolfe is a product tester, writer, and serial DIYer. When he isn’t writing, he spends his time upgrading, repairing, and replacing anything and everything in his home, yard, and garden. According to recent reports, A right-angle drill solves problems when a standard drill can’t reach—navigating between studs, working inside cabinets, or tackling tight corners. While this makes these specialized power tools handy in these situations, who truly needs a right-angle drill?

It has been revealed that plumbers, electricians, carpenters, and pretty much anyone involved in construction and renovation projects will appreciate having one handy. Even hobbyists and homeowners may need a right-angle drill when tackling certain jobs, such as installing cabinetry or assembling furniture.

We test the top right-angle drills to find the best models for pros and homeowners. Our favorite was the Ridgid thanks to its comprehensive kit, durable build, and impressive power. Below, find the results of our hands-on tests and learn how these models earned their spot in this lineup of the best right-angle drills.

Any of the following right-angle drills will make it easier to drill holes and drive screws in tight areas, but each one comes with some pros and cons. We’ve detailed both the benefits and the downsides noted during our tests. Some models are best suited to light-duty use, while others are powerhouses designed with construction pros in mind. There’s sure to be one that will suit your project needs.

Ridgid’s cordless right-angle drill manages to be compact and lightweight while still offering  tremendous drilling and driving power.

It has been revealed that its head measures just 3.5 inches long, making it one of the shortest 18V or 20V angle drills we tested. Couple that with its slim profile and short length, and it fits easily into tight spaces inside cabinets and under-sink vanities.

Industry observers note that right-angle drills tend to be top-heavy, which can make them awkward to hold. With its compact size and light weight, the Ridgid was an exception. It felt comfortable and well balanced in the hand, which is significant given that these tools are often used in tight spaces where it’s not possible to get a two-handed grip. Adding to its maneuverability is a long trigger that’s easy to access from various hand positions. The trigger has ample rubberized grip, making it easy to keep a firm hold on the tool.

According to recent reports, given its smaller size, we expected it to come up lacking in power. It didn’t. With a max speed of 1,900 RPM, the Ridgid had no trouble handling the larger bits we tested, easily boring holes with a 1/2-inch twist bit and 1-inch spade bit. It followed up that impressive performance by effortlessly driving ten 3-inch carpenter screws into a couple of stacked 2x4s. And if you need additional torque, you can get its max 375 in-lbs (inch-pounds) by dropping down to its lower speed setting.

Industry observers note that what our tester indicates: “Ridgid’s right-angle drill is everything you want out of this kind of specialty power tool. It’s compact and lightweight while still packing plenty of power for drilling large holes and driving fasteners.”—Tony Carrick, Product Reviews tester and writer.

Get the Ridgid right-angle drill at The Home Depot.

Ryobi’s tools have steadily grown more powerful over the years, slowly closing the gap with premium brands, and the PSBRA02 right-angled drill is a great example of the brand’s progression. With a max speed of 1,700 RPM and 350 in-lbs of torque, it can handle just about any job that requires this type of tool. Those specs also put it in the same ballpark as other cordless drills, all at a friendlier price point for DIYers who may not need premium performance.

Recent findings suggest that it produced enough power for drilling ½-inch holes with a twist bit and 1-inch holes with a paddle bit. It also didn’t struggle to drive a 3-inch carpentry screw through two 2x4s. The PSBRA02 won’t win any speed tests, but unless you’re drilling dozens of holes or driving loads of screws, you likely won’t notice the time difference.

The PSBRA02 isn’t the most compact right-angle drill out there, nor is it the largest. Nonetheless, it fits into compact spaces thanks to a head that measures just 3.5 inches long. It also feels comfortable in the hand with a manageable weight, plenty of rubberized grip around the handle, and a long trigger accessible from various hand positions.

Get the Ryobi right-angle drill at Amazon or The Home Depot.

Looking for a 12-volt right-angle drill that delivers impressive power? The Milwaukee cordless drill caught our attention for all the right reasons. We tested the kit version of this small right-angle drill, complete with a battery and charger. However, users who already own 12V Milwaukee tools can order the drill as a “tool only” and utilize existing batteries.

This drill sits on the smaller side of the spectrum, weighing in at a mere 2.03 pounds. It slipped effortlessly into tight spots during tests, and its lightweight design let us comfortably operate it with just one hand. Since this drill packs less power than some other models we tested, it isn’t well-suited for heavy construction work. Instead, it excels at light-duty tasks like furniture assembly and drilling small holes in confined spaces. The integrated LED light was handy, though we did use an additional work light in darker areas.

The real surprise here is the inclusion of a clutch, an essential feature that prevents stripping screw heads. What’s more, the elongated trigger design allowed us to adjust our grip up or down on the tool handle (based on comfort level) and still easily pull the trigger. While this drill is not intended for heavy-duty tasks, it’s a good choice for electricians, HVAC technicians, and plumbers who require precise screw insertion or minor hole drilling in tight spaces.

Get the Milwaukee right-angle drill at Amazon (tool only), Ace Hardware (tool only), or The Home Depot (battery included).

Look no further than the Bosch 12V Flexiclick drill. This handy tool boasts high and low speeds alongside a variable-speed trigger, and it performed admirably in our hands-on tests.

It has been revealed that unlike other 12V models, the Bosch Flexiclick isn’t confined solely to right-angle drilling. The array of attachments sets this drill apart, transforming it into a standard, offset, or right-angle drill by simply connecting the corresponding attachment.

Recent findings suggest that one of our favorite features was the head’s ability to rotate in any direction. This allowed us to insert fasteners at any angle, though it required two hands when using the rotating head. Weighing only 1.2 pounds, this drill is comfortable for extended use, yet it offers an impressive 1,750 RPM—a remarkable feat for a 12-volt model. For DIY enthusiasts and shoppers seeking versatility without the need for heavy torque, the Bosch Flexiclick is a game changer. We found it effortless to change attachments thanks to the one-click interface, and it offers the ability to use the drill in multiple ways. A convenient storage case keeps everything organized.

It has been revealed that introducing the powerhouse of right-angle drills: The Makita DA4031. This electric drill stands out as a true performer. While it’s the only corded right-angle drill we tested, a host of impressive features make it an outstanding choice for construction pros.

In a recent development, this heavy-duty drill features a potent 10-amp motor that provided unwavering power in our tests, drilling effortlessly through wall studs and joists. We found the second-hand handle indispensable for robust drilling tasks, as it let us grip it firmly while drilling for additional support. Perhaps best of all, both our right- and left-handed testers were able to use the drill comfortably, thanks to the ability to attach the handle to either side of the tool.

Industry observers note that the corded Makita made quick work of drilling large holes through ply materials and dimensional lumber. Its built-in clutch exhibited impeccable performance, effectively halting torque at low speeds when the tool met heavy resistance. With a drill this powerful, a good clutch is a must—not just to avoid stripping screw heads, but to keep you from breaking a wrist.

Sources indicate that while the corded design offers a consistent power supply sans battery charging, it has limitations. Since we’re so used to cordless tools, we really noticed the Makita’s cord limitations, like having to drag a cord around and being limited to working near an electrical outlet.

For those seeking the ultimate right-angle drilling companion on the jobsite, it’s tough to beat the Makita DA4031 for its heavy-duty construction, durability, and reliable performance.

Get the Makita DA4031 right-angle drill at Amazon or Acme Tools.

DeWalt’s 20V MAX right-angle cordless drill packs plenty of power, though this brawn comes at the cost of its maneuverability in confined spaces. Still, the DCD740 blazed through our drilling tests. With its high speed and torque output, it bored a clean hole with a ½-inch twist bit and chipped out a surprisingly smooth 1-inch hole with a paddle bit. It was also a fast driver, sinking 3-inch carpentry screws faster than other cordless right-angle drills we tested.

It has been revealed that the DeWalt DCD740 has two speeds, so you can drop the speed down to max out the torque, which will help prevent stripping out screw heads. Along with its power output, the DCD740 also has a tougher feel than other right-angle drills with a metal chuck and thicker plastic housing.

In a recent development, the DCD740 is one of the brand’s earliest 20V cordless tools. It uses a brushed motor and is larger and heavier than other right-angle drills. Its bare tool weight of just over 3 pounds may not sound like a lot, but it makes a difference when extending your arm to drive in a screw in the deeper recesses of a cabinet. Its larger body and longer head mean it won’t fit into as tight a space as other more compact models. Still, it’s a powerful right-angle drill and a great option for anyone who already owns a few DeWalt 20V cordless tools.

What our tester says: “This may be one of DeWalt’s oldest cordless tools, but it packs more driving and drilling power than other cordless right-angle drills we tested.”—Tony Carrick, Product Reviews tester and writer.

Get the DeWalt DCD 740 at Lowe’s.

DeWalt’s handy right-angle attachment offers a creative solution for those who occasionally need access to confined spaces without buying a dedicated right-angle drill.

This ingenious accessory is not a stand-alone tool but a versatile addition that easily connects to the chuck of a ¼-inch standard DeWalt drill/driver or impact driver. It is well suited to even the tightest of spots and offers a convenient means of right-angle drilling and driving. As staunch admirers of DeWalt’s innovation and craftsmanship, we think this compact attachment lives up to the manufacturer’s stellar reputation.

With the attachment connected to a standard drill, we easily drilled in tight spaces where our hands could barely fit. Although designed for light-duty applications, its practicality is undeniable. Since the attachment is made from fully magnetized and durable materials, we were able to insert screws in tight spots without needing to wedge in a second hand to hold the screw steady.

This small attachment weighs just 4.8 ounces and can be stored alongside a standard drill, so it’s always ready to take the place of a hand ratchet for quick fastener attachment or drilling within confined areas. The DeWalt attachment also works well when connected to a standard drill.

Get the DeWalt right-angle drill attachment at Amazon or Lowe’s.

We tested the drills’ capabilities in drilling holes through various materials, including studs and joists, to simulate the challenges faced during electrical and plumbing work. Recent findings suggest that throughout our testing, we paid close attention to the drills’ power, precision, and ease of use. We evaluated their power and performance to gauge their ability to handle different tasks efficiently. Finally, we awarded points based on a rubric: The better a tool performed a task, the more points it received. After testing, we averaged the points to help determine the best uses for the different tools.

According to recent reports, the width of the head is perhaps the most crucial feature of a right-angle drill because it determines the space into which it can fit. However, there are several other key factors to take into account, including motor speed, power source, and weight. Ahead, learn more about these and other important attributes to think about when choosing the best right-angle drill.

It has been revealed that right-angle drills come in corded and cordless varieties, each with its own pros and cons. Cordless drills run on a rechargeable lithium-ion battery and offer the convenience and flexibility of not needing an electrical outlet or a cord. This lets you use them virtually anywhere.

It has been revealed that corded models, in comparison, require a standard electrical outlet. While these drills aren’t as convenient, a 120V power supply makes them more powerful while providing a reliable and constant power supply. Corded drills are also generally less expensive than cordless models. As with many power tools, spending more on a cordless model makes sense if it will see regular use. A less expensive corded model should suffice for DIYers who may use a right-angle drill only occasionally.

Size and weight determine a right-angle drill’s functionality and ease of use. Because a right-angle drill is meant to fit into tight spaces, size is crucial. Most right-angle drills have a head between 3 and 4 inches wide, so they can reach places standard corded and cordless power drills can’t.

Right-angle drills can also be short and lightweight enough to manage with one hand—although heavy-duty models typically come with a secondary handle.

Chuck size is also crucial. Most right-angle drills have a ⅜-inch chuck, which helps keep the head compact. Some larger models feature a ½-inch chuck for drilling larger holes or driving in bigger screws. These models typically have a wider head.

Right-angle drills have ergonomically shaped handles with rubberized grips that let you hold them securely with one hand while drilling. Many also have detachable side handles that let you apply more leverage with the other hand. Some manufacturers equip right-angle drills with paddle-style triggers that run the length of the handle. This feature lets you better regulate trigger pressure to control the drill’s speed.

A drill’s speed determines how swiftly the tool can drill holes or drive screws. It also gives an indication of how much torque the drill produces if the manufacturer does not provide that information. Speed is measured in RPM and, in most cases, is directly related to the power source. Most cordless 18V right-angle drills top out at around 1,500 RPM, while some 20V drills can reach about 2,000 RPM.

According to recent reports, corded right-angle drills have access to more power, which means they can produce more RPM. A corded 4-amp right-angle drill boasts around 2,400 RPM. While speed isn’t the same as torque, motors that can produce higher RPM are more powerful and thus capable of producing more torque.

Industry observers note that when assessing a cordless tool’s battery life, consider not only how long each charge lasts but also how long the battery itself will hold a charge before it needs replacing. Most batteries for right-angle cordless drills will last about 3 hours on a single charge with intermittent use and will take about 3 hours to recharge.

Industry observers note that lithium-ion batteries typically last about 3 years, or about 300 to 500 charging cycles, before they begin to lose their ability to hold a charge. This doesn’t mean the battery will stop working altogether. As a battery nears the end of its life, it will simply last for a shorter period of time and require more frequent charging.

Industry observers note that as with standard drills, right-angle drills are capable of using various types of bits and attachments. These drills are adept at drilling holes with standard drill bits or driving in screws with Phillips-head, flat, star, and other styles of screw-driving bits. These drills can also use socket attachments to drive bolts. Like other power tools, right-angle drills use a variety of accessories, including drill bits, screwdriver bits, chuck keys, and other accessories that can be misplaced. For this reason, many right-angle drills include a storage bag that holds the tool, accessories, batteries, and chargers all in one place for easy storage and transport.

Right-angle drills also often offer convenient features like LED lights that illuminate the work area and switches that make it easier to control the drill speed, permitting the user to increase or decrease the speed range to maximize control and improve torque.

For more information on how and where to best use a right-angle drill, read on for answers to some common questions about these power tools.

A right-angle drill has a geared head that rotates the chuck 90 degrees from the body’s axis, letting it reach tight spaces and drill or drive at angles a conventional drill can’t.

According to recent reports, this versatile tool is helpful for a wide range of projects. It can be invaluable for fitting into tight spaces when working on a vehicle. A right-angle drill is also ideal for drilling between floor joists or wall studs, which are spaces that are typically too narrow for a standard drill.

It has been revealed that A ⅜-inch drill has a chuck that can accommodate drill bits up to ⅜ inch. Similarly, a ½-inch drill has a larger chuck that can handle drill bits with a maximum diameter of ½ inch. A ½-inch drill generally offers more power and torque, making it suitable for drilling larger holes and tackling tougher materials. It’s commonly used in construction and heavy-duty applications.

A right-angle drill attachment is an accessory that can be added to a standard drill or driver to enable drilling and driving in tight or confined spaces that are difficult to access with a regular tool.

Yes. A right-angle drill can handle drilling tasks that require high torque and speed, depending on the type of drill. A model drill such as the Makita DA4031 or DeWalt DCD740 can drill large holes through floor joists, wall studs, and framing plates with ease.

In a recent development, most cordless drills don’t require you to do a lot to maintain them, but there are few things you can do to keep them in tip-top shape. Wipe off any sawdust or debris after each use, paying close attention to the chuck and air vents. Remove the battery when the drill isn’t in use and store it in a cool place. Lubricate the chuck periodically by applying a small amount of machine oil to the chuck jaws to prevent stiffness.

The biggest danger with a right-angle drill is sudden kickback that can cause wrist injuries. If possible use two hands when operating a right-angle drill, one to control the trigger and the other on the back of the head to stabilize its motion. If that isn’t possible, brace the drill body or your arm against a solid object, like a wall stud, to prevent the tool from spinning out if it jams.

Bad Habits That Are Making Your Wood Deck Rot

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Industry observers note that A wooden deck adds charm to a backyard and serves as the ultimate backdrop for outdoor relaxation, but keeping it in prime condition requires some work. While weather certainly takes a toll, some habits you might practice unwittingly could be accelerating deck rot. We spoke to a couple of deck experts to identify common maintenance missteps, from aggressive pressure washing and harsh chemical cleaners to trapped moisture under potted plants and forgotten debris. By identifying these mistakes and adopting safer maintenance techniques, you can protect your deck from premature decay and preserve it for years to come.

One of the biggest mistakes homeowners make when it comes to wooden deck care is pressure-washing it too aggressively, which often strips the wood fibers, splinters the wood, and leaves permanent marks, states Jon Colbasiuc, owner of Supreme Deck Store in Helmetta, New Jersey. When the wood splinters, it opens up recesses where mold can start to grow. This can eventually damage the wood grain, force dirt deeper into the wood’s surface, make it harder to keep the deck clean, and shorten the lifespan of the wood. Instead, Colbasiuc recommends using a soft-bristled brush with deck-specific cleaner, or pressure washing the deck from an adequate distance on a low-pressure water setting.

Another common issue is letting leaves, dirt, dust, pollen, and other debris build up between deck boards, which can trap moisture and eventually lead to mildew or rotting, notes Jake Anderson of Modernize It LLC in Candia, New Hampshire. It’s vital to regularly sweep the deck with a stiff-bristle brush to keep it clear of such materials. “Regularly cleaning between the boards helps maintain adequate drainage and airflow, especially in the fall when leaves are a more prominent issue,” adds Colbasiuc.

It has been revealed that using a putty knife or special deck gap tool, clean the gaps between deck boards at least twice per season during spring and fall. Even covered decks can have debris that gathers in corners. Trim vegetation that’s within 12 inches of the deck to minimize leaves, berries, and other plant materials from falling onto the deck.

Featuring a telescoping handle and a narrow hook on one end, this tool allows you to clean between deck boards while standing.

Recent findings suggest that it might seem like a good idea to clean a deck with chlorine bleach, but you should avoid using bleach. The cleaner can be very corrosive, which will discolor the wood, and end up destroying the wood’s natural lignin, which can ruin its strength and structure. The bleach also raises the pH of the wood surface, which can make it harder for stains and sealants to work properly in the future. Finally, the bleach can ruin metal objects used on the deck, such as nails, screws, and fasteners. Instead, clean the deck using a nontoxic oxygenated cleaner with an oxalic acid-based wood brightener.

Another common mistake is leaving items out on the deck for long periods of time. “Rugs, planters, and other items sitting against the wood can trap moisture beneath them, which accelerates discoloration and deterioration of the wood,” warns Colbasiuc. This can lead to stains, moss growth, and deck rot. Instead, he recommends choosing breathable rugs specifically meant for outdoor use, elevating a plant container with planter feet, and moving the furniture every so often to help the wood dry between rains.

It has been revealed that you’ll also want to avoid doing anything that can scratch the surface of the wood. A common blunder is sliding around patio furniture with metal legs that can scrape the deck. Either lift the furniture when moving it or add protective pads. “Using metal shovels can scratch wood, create splinters, and scrape away at protective finishes,” notes Colbasiuc. “Instead, use plastic-edged shovels, which are a safer option to clear snow from the deck.”.

It has been revealed that I meant to send this story a bit ago when you were discussing those scary old Milwaukee right-angle drills. Mike really knocked it out of the park with his story about a person spinning under a truck. My story is on par, though I didn’t see it first hand.

Sources indicate that an electrician I worked with had a right-angle drill mishap that stands out as one of the greatest, mostly harmless construction stories I’ve heard. He was standing on an upside-down bucket reaching and drilling upward into the ceiling area with a right-angle drill. You see where this is going, right?

According to recent reports, the drill stuck on something, kicked back, and it twisted him off of the bucket. When the bucket tipped he was left hanging by the drill and holding onto the trigger. He spun, dangling in the air, until the cord wrapped around him enough to unplug itself. If I remember correctly, his partner had to help extract him from the situation.

I sold my right-angle drill to an electrician recently because I hadn’t used it in 10 years due to fear of injury. That was the scariest tool in my carpentry arsenal, not the spinning blade tools.

To the disembodied voices telling me to buy more tools,.

Are active radon mitigation systems creating radon mines? Does constant suction create defined pathways for more nearby radon to escape the ground? In my 1946 Pleasant Grove, Utah, house I have a partially completed radon mitigation system. It is right now just sucking air from the unencapsulated crawlspace. I’m actively monitoring radon level, and they stay below the 4 picocuries-per-liter threshold while the fan is on.

Recent findings suggest that I turned the radon fan off temporarily. When I finally noticed the radon levels creeping back up, they were much higher than ever before (including before installing the fan). That’s what made me wonder about this idea of creating an easier channel for the radon.

I’m renovating an entire house in Rochester, Newly introduced York, and have an insulation question about the ceiling of a mid-1980s addition.

Sources indicate that when I bought the house, the ceiling had Sheetrock with significant sags between the 24-in.-o.c. framing, including one much wider sag in a single bay. I removed the Sheetrock and found the ceiling cavities packed tightly with cellulose, which was weighing down very stretched-out poly sheeting. I also found a roughly 42-in. span with no framing (related to old skylights, I believe). I’ve since had all the cellulose removed and am starting fresh.

It has been revealed that the roof is a vented assembly with a ridge vent and several soffit vents on each side, but there were no rafter/insulation baffles. I’m wondering whether there was ever meaningful soffit-to-ridge airflow through the roof cavities.

The existing roof sheathing is also in mediocre condition. There aren’t active leaks, but I expect to replace the sheathing when I redo the roof down the road.

That leads me to a few questions:.

I’ve attached a Google Drive folder with photos that should illustrate the situation: https://photos.app.goo.gl/TGeTmNWneBXaFhpi7.

Thanks in advance, and I love the pod!
