#67348. Breaking: Justices Thomas and Alito on State Requirements That Continuing Professional Education Discuss Certain Topics

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2055 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Justices Thomas and Alito on State Requirements That Continuing Professional Education Discuss Certain Topics

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, from Justice Thomas's dissent from denial of certiorari today in Khatibi v.
  • In 2022, California began requiring private instructors in privately run and privately accredited continuing medical education (CME) courses to discuss how so-called implicit bias affects healthcare outcomes.
  • It has been revealed that I would have granted certiorari to clarify the government-speech doctrine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, from Justice Thomas's dissent from denial of certiorari today in Khatibi v. Yip, joined by Justice Alito (Justice Gorsuch voted to grant the petition, but didn't sign on to the dissent):.

In 2022, California began requiring private instructors in privately run and privately accredited continuing medical education (CME) courses to discuss how so-called implicit bias affects healthcare outcomes. The Ninth Circuit held that First Amendment scrutiny did not apply to this compelled-speech requirement because the breadth of California's CME regulation renders the content of any CME course government speech, not private speech. That logic fundamentally misunderstands this Court's precedents and the Constitution. First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.

It has been revealed that I would have granted certiorari to clarify the government-speech doctrine. At a minimum, the Ninth Circuit misapplied Shurtleff v. Boston (2022), which instructs courts to identify government speech by considering (1) "the history of the expression at issue," (2) "the public's likely perception as to who (the government or a private person) is speaking," and (3) "the extent to which the government has actively shaped or controlled the expression." The Ninth Circuit collapsed those distinct inquiries, focusing on the breadth of the government's regulatory scheme at each step. More fundamentally, however, Shurtleff is leading courts astray.

I joined Justice ALITO's concurrence in Shurtleff, which warned that the majority's three-factor test could cause courts to conclude that extensive government regulation transforms a private message into government speech exempt from First Amendment scrutiny. As the Ninth Circuit's decision reveals, those concerns were prescient. This Court should reconsider whether the Shurtleff test is the proper mode of analysis for identifying government speech….

It has been revealed that california-licensed physicians are required to complete 50 hours of approved CME every two years. Credit-eligible CME courses are often organized by private entities, certified by private accreditors, and taught by private instructors. The State does not preapprove course content but reserves the right to audit courses for compliance with its CME standards.

The Medical Board of California "adopt[s] and administer[s] [CME] standards," few of which relate to course content. In addition, the State requires that CME courses broadly relate to the medical profession. They must "serve to maintain, develop, or increase the knowledge, skills, and professional performance that a physician and surgeon uses to provide care, or to improve the quality of care provided to patients." In 2019, however, the California Legislature added a requirement that after January 1, 2022, all CME courses must "contain curriculum that includes the understanding of implicit bias." To satisfy that requirement, CME courses must contain "[e]xamples of how implicit bias affects perceptions and treatment decisions of physicians and surgeons, leading to disparities in health outcomes" or "[s]trategies to address how unintended biases in decisionmaking may contribute to health care disparities.".

Petitioners Dr. Azadeh Khatibi and Do No Harm do not want to speak California's preferred message on implicit bias, and they challenged § 2190.1(d) as compelling speech in violation of the First Amendment. Dr. Khatibi, a California-licensed ophthalmologist, creates and teaches CME courses. She "disagrees that implicit bias is the primary factor driving disparities in healthcare" and does not want to devote time to the subject during her courses. Do No Harm is a nonprofit corporation. At least one of its members teaches CME courses and believes that implicit bias trainings "have not been shown to successfully reduce barriers to healthcare, and instead risk infecting healthcare decisions with divisive and discriminatory ideas." Yet, California's implicit-bias-training requirement leaves petitioners no choice but to discuss the topic in a way that affirms the State's view that implicit bias causes "disparities in health outcomes…..

Sources indicate that the Ninth Circuit held that all three Shurtleff factors indicate that "CMEs eligible for Board credit constitute government speech." At every step of the analysis, the Ninth Circuit emphasized the breadth of the State's regulation. Considering history, the court noted that California "has long regulated the practice of medicine as an exercise of the police power" and has "adopted, updated, and enforced CME standards." Considering the public's likely perception of the speaker in a CME course, the court reasoned that "licensees could attribute approved CMEs' content to California" because "their profession is heavily regulated." Considering the extent to which the government has shaped the expression, the court cited "California's extraordinary control over accredited CMEs." As Judge VanDyke explained in his dissent from the denial of rehearing en banc, the panel's "approach boil[ed] down to a single-factor analysis: does the government 'heavily' or 'actively' regulate CMEs?" ….

In its blinkered application of the Shurtleff factors, the Ninth Circuit lost sight of the core government-speech inquiry: whether the government is "speak[ing] for itself or … regulat[ing] private expression.".

According to recent reports, the government-speech doctrine occupies a narrow corner of our First Amendment jurisprudence. The First Amendment protects the people's right of free speech against government interference; it does not prevent the government from speaking for itself. "But courts must be very careful when a government claims that speech by one or more private speakers is actually government speech." "If private speech could be passed off as government speech by simply affixing a government seal of approval, government could … muffle the expression of disfavored viewpoints," or, as here, require private speakers to convey government messages without facing any constitutional scrutiny.

This Court has thus exercised "great caution" before characterizing a message as government speech. In Johanns v. Livestock Marketing Assn (2005), we held that government-sponsored beef ads constituted government speech because the government determined "the overarching message" of the ads, helped develop proposals for the ads, reviewed every ad "for substance and for wording," and the Secretary of Agriculture "exercise[d] final approval authority over every word used in every" ad. In Pleasant Grove City v. Summum (2009), we held that the permanent display of monuments in a public park was government speech because the City "effectively controlled the messages sent by the monuments in the Park by exercising final approval authority over their selection." And, in Walker v. Texas Div., Sons of Confederate Veterans, Inc. (2015), we held that the messages on government-issued license plates, over which the State "maintain[ed] direct control," were government speech.

Recent findings suggest that since Walker—which we have described as the "outer boun[d] of the government-speech doctrine," Matal v. Tam (2017)—we have been careful to distinguish between government control over messages and government control over the broader scheme through which the messages are communicated. We held, for example, that trademarks are private speech, notwithstanding the government's substantial involvement in the registration process. And, this Court held that flags flown outside of Boston's City Hall did not constitute government speech in part because the city regularly permitted private groups to freely fly their own colors. In all these cases, the controlling question was whether "the government intends to speak for itself or to regulate private expression.".

Put in those simple terms, and in light of our precedents, California's attempt to require private individuals in privately accredited CME courses to run implicit-bias training is an evident attempt "to regulate private expression." … First, California has not historically used CME to communicate government messages. While the State requires that CME courses generally relate to the practice of medicine and occasionally requires that courses cover certain subjects, California has not otherwise dictated the content of courses.

Recent findings suggest that second, because California "relie[s] on the participation of private parties in executing the CME scheme," the public is unlikely to perceive a private instructor's CME course as government speech. As the Ninth Circuit acknowledged, Dr. Khatibi "plausibly alleged facts suggesting that attendees treat her as the person responsible for CME content.".

Third, while California extensively regulates the medical field, licenses physicians, and sets the requirements for credit-eligible CME, there is little evidence that California "shape[s] the messages" communicated in CME courses. Despite its long recitation of California regulations, the Ninth Circuit did not identify any state law that requires private speakers in a CME course to express a particular viewpoint—even on contestable medical challenges. The implicit-bias-training requirement is a notable departure from that practice. It should have been easy, then, for the courts below to conclude that California's implicit-bias-training requirement regulates private speech.

More troubling than the Ninth Circuit's misapplication of the Shurtleff factors are the implications of the court's decision. On the Ninth Circuit's view of government speech, could California require a CME instructor to communicate the State's preferred message on the availability of abortion? Could the State require a CME instructor to inform participants that for certain patients, gender-transition surgery is ethically required?

Recent findings suggest that what of other professions whose members California licenses and regulates? At the next statewide legal conference at which lectures are offered for continuing legal education, could California require a keynote speaker to oppose racial preferences in law firm hiring? Applying the Ninth Circuit's logic, enough government regulation of the field would convert the private speaker's message in each of these hypotheticals into government speech unprotected by the First Amendment. That result does not follow from this Court's precedents, and it certainly does not follow from the Constitution….

According to recent reports, if the Ninth Circuit's decision is truly the kind of result that Shurtleff's three-factor test countenances, we should reconsider Shurtleff. Before Shurtleff, this Court had identified history, public perception, and government control as "relevant" but not mandatory "considerations" for identifying government speech. When Shurtleff described those considerations as a three-factor test, several Members of the Court—myself included—warned that the test would be unworkable and obscure the central inquiry in government-speech cases: whether the government is speaking or regulating private speech. "[L]ike any factorized analysis," the Shurtleff majority's approach does not "provide a principled way of deciding cases." Worse, myopic focus on the history and scope of government control over speech may give courts the false impression that state regulation can convert private speech into government speech.

After only a few years, those concerns are materializing. The Ninth Circuit relied on California's regulation of CME to conclude that requiring private speakers to communicate a government message was not compelled speech but government speech. That is precisely the paradox predicted by the concurrence in Shurtleff: that "government action that regulates private speech would" now "qualify as government speech unregulated by the First Amendment." But, neither compelled speech nor "[c]ensorship" are "made constitutional by aggressive and direct application." It cannot be the case that compelled speech becomes government speech because the government has compelled the speech.

I would grant certiorari to correct course. In my view, the relevant inquiry in a government-speech case is straightforward: Is the government "speaking," or is it "regulating private expression"? The challenged government activity must be "government speech in the literal sense—purposeful communication of a governmentally determined message by a person acting within the scope of a power to speak for the government." Moreover, "the government must … not rely on a means that abridges the speech of persons acting in a private capacity," because doing so reveals that the government has moved from the role of speaker to that of regulator.

Under this framework, it is easy to see why California's law is subject to First Amendment scrutiny. The State's implicit-bias-training requirement is not speech by any government actor; it is a requirement that private speakers communicate certain messages. Although the government may "deputiz[e] private persons as its agents" to convey its message, Dr. Khatibi and Do No Harm's members have not "voluntarily assumed" "a public or quasi-public capacity that empowers them to speak on behalf of the government." They share their own messages through the CME courses they create and deliver, and they do so in their private capacities. Even "government speech in the literal sense is not exempt from First Amendment attack if it uses a means that restricts private expression," such as "compelled speech." When, as here, the government does not issue its own messages but instead requires private speakers to communicate the government's viewpoint, the First Amendment applies….

It has been revealed that A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny. We should not permit the government-speech doctrine to be wielded as "a cover for censorship" or a cloak for compelled speech.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface.
  • According to recent reports, ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.

Ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface. Applying ice melt to certain materials can cause significant damage and should be avoided. Ahead, learn which surfaces are most vulnerable to damage from ice melt, why it happens and what safer alternatives you can use to keep outdoor areas free from ice.

According to recent reports, ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage. The type of damage will depend on the surface and how it interacts with ice melt.

Ice melt contains rock salt, calcium chloride and/or magnesium chloride to melt ice faster and at lower temperatures. While all melting salt is corrosive and can damage outdoor surfaces, ice melt products can react differently than rock salt alone.

Sources indicate that ice melt seeps deeply into porous cement-based materials. The calcium chloride in ice melt can react with elements of concrete or brick to form calcium oxychloride crystals. As the crystals grow, they generate extreme pressure that can cause cracks, surface spalling and crumbling.

According to recent reports, de-icing products accelerate freeze-thaw cycles in porous cement-based surfaces, causing them to break down. “It makes the freezing and thawing cycle more aggressive, which is what causes the surface to break up,” Murphy claims.

Though less damaging than rock salt, ice melt can still contribute to deterioration. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride attract and retain moisture, increasing the potential for freeze-thaw damage.

Conversely, ice melt draws moisture out of organic materials, causing them to dry out. Over time, this moisture loss can lead to warping, cracking, splitting and other forms of deterioration.

Industry observers note that ice melt accelerates metal oxidation to create rust. It can corrode rebar embedded in concrete, potentially causing cracks and structural damage, as well as rusting exposed metal stairs and railings.

It’s best to avoid applying salt to these salt-sensitive surfaces.

“Latest concrete is the most vulnerable because it takes weeks to fully cure, so salt on the surface will cause the top few millimeters to flake off,” Murphy indicates. To be safe, avoid salting new concrete for the first season.

“Cracked concrete opens up for water to get inside, and salt in the water will only make that worse because it will freeze and thaw more aggressively,” Murphy says.

It has been revealed that all ice melt products will damage hard-scape surfaces due to chemical reactions and freeze-thaw cycles. “If you are using them, use them sparingly and remove them as soon as possible to decrease continuous exposure for your hardscape areas,” Zurcher says.

Natural stone like limestone and flagstone can react to ice melt compounds. The porous surface is vulnerable to damaging freeze-thaw cycles as well.

Harsh de-icers can damage dyed, painted or stamped concrete surfaces by breaking down color pigments.

Metal stairs and railings will rapidly rust when salt is applied to them, so it’s best to avoid it.

According to recent reports, ice melt draws moisture from wood, causing cracking, warping and raised fibers. It also degrades paint and stain and leaves behind chalky white salt stains.

Sand: Sand doesn’t melt ice, but does provide traction to prevent slips.

Wood ash: Instead of throwing away wood ash, use it as a salt alternative to melt ice and also provide improved traction.

Electric mats: Installed before cold weather sets in, electric melting mats warm up and prevent ice from ever forming. These can be very effective on stairs and sidewalks.

Weed torch: Weed torches are handy when you need to melt a lot of ice swiftly. Do not use one to melt ice on wood and avoid painted or stained concrete as well.

It has been revealed that “The best way to reduce damage from these chemicals is to shovel snow as soon as possible,” Zurcher indicates, so you can use less of them. Use ice melt sparingly, and only as directed. A handful is enough to treat three square yards. Instead of using ice melt alone, mix a small amount with sand to treat surfaces.

Regular sealing protects cement-based products. “Reseal every three to five years to make sure no water can get in, salty or not,” Murphy indicates. Additionally, use chloride-free de-icing products, or those labelled as “concrete-safe”.

Newly poured concrete is the most vulnerable to salt damage, but all concrete surfaces will experience damage with enough prolonged exposure to salt.

It depends on the extent of the damage. Major cracks and breakage mean concrete needs to be removed and repoured, Zurcher claims, while surface damage could be skim-coated, with potentially limited results.

Pet-safe products will have similar effects on hardscape areas, Zurcher says, as they still contain salt.

Justice Thomas on the Second Amendment in "Sensitive Places"

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that from Justice Thomas's statement respecting the denial of certiorari in Novotny v.
  • According to recent reports, maryland is one of several States that prohibit law-abiding gun owners from carrying firearms in a wide variety of public places.
  • I am skeptical that each of these laws "is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" in "sensitive places." Still, I agree with the Court's decision not to grant certiorari.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that from Justice Thomas's statement respecting the denial of certiorari in Novotny v. Moore:.

According to recent reports, maryland is one of several States that prohibit law-abiding gun owners from carrying firearms in a wide variety of public places. Under Maryland law, an individual may not carry a firearm in public demonstrations, mass transit, places of amusement, healthcare facilities, locations that sell alcohol for onsite consumption, and tens of thousands of acres of state park and forest land. The Fourth Circuit upheld these restrictions against petitioners' Second Amendment challenge because it concluded that each law banned firearms in a "sensitive place.".

I am skeptical that each of these laws "is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" in "sensitive places." Still, I agree with the Court's decision not to grant certiorari. Because each Maryland statute implicates a distinct historical tradition of firearm regulation, the breadth of petitioners' challenge would complicate our review. In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however, we should consider the scope of States' authority to ban firearms in "sensitive places.".

The Second Amendment recognizes the people's "inherent" right to keep and bear firearms, a right that admits of only historically grounded exceptions. Before and after the founding, it was well understood that individuals enjoyed a natural right to keep and bear arms, which included the right to carry firearms in public spaces for self-defense. The Constitution "codified [that] pre-existing right." The first generations after the founding recognized the breadth of the Second Amendment's "guarante[e]," and "those who sought to carry firearms publicly and peaceably in antebellum America were generally free to do so." Thus, when a State seeks to restrict the right to bear arms—including by limiting the places in which a law-abiding citizen may carry his firearm—the State must root its law in the Second Amendment's "historical understanding" by "demonstrat[ing] that the regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation.".

Sources indicate that this Court has previously acknowledged a limited tradition of States' regulating the right to carry firearms in certain "sensitive places." In Bruen, we observed that early American legislatures sometimes prohibited weapons in "legislative assemblies, polling places, and courthouses." But, we emphasized that this tradition was narrow. "[T]he historical record yields relatively few 18th- and 19th-century 'sensitive places' where weapons were altogether prohibited." While "courts can use analogies to those historical regulations of 'sensitive places' to determine that modern regulations … are constitutionally permissible," "expanding the category of 'sensitive places' … to all places of public congregation … would eviscerate the general right to publicly carry arms for self-defense.".

It has been revealed that nevertheless, States have seized on the idea of "sensitive places" to prohibit the peaceable carry of firearms in locations that bear little resemblance to legislatures, polling places, or courthouses. Latest Jersey, for example, prohibits firearms in at least 25 locations, including zoos, public libraries, casinos, and state-owned beaches. New York has designated 20 locations as "sensitive," ranging from "any place of worship" to "residential settings licensed … by the department of health." California's 29 gun-free spaces include "athletic facilit[ies]," "financial institution[s]," and any government-permitted "public gathering or special event." {Several other States ban firearms in many public places.} These restrictions stand on questionable historical ground. And, their cumulative effect is to prohibit firearms wherever people gather for eating, drinking, recreation, amusement, and free speech—an affront to the right of "law-abiding citizens" to "carr[y] arms in public for" their "ordinary self-defense.".

According to recent reports, the lower courts have largely blessed these ahistorical ventures. The Fourth Circuit below upheld all but one of Maryland's locational restrictions. A now-vacated decision of the Third Circuit upheld many of New Jersey's "sensitive-place" laws. Courts of Appeals have also rejected challenges to specific locational restrictions in New York, California, and Hawaii.

In a recent development, I harbor serious doubts that our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation supports many of these sweeping restrictions. In an appropriate case, this Court should consider whether particular sensitive-place laws are consistent with the right to public carry.

Recent findings suggest that don’t wait until temperatures plummet to perform basic electric and gas furnace maintenance and cleaning. By performing basic furnace cleaning and maintenance tasks now, you can avoid the expensive inconvenience (and danger) of leaving your family without heat during the coldest part of the year. You can also actually prolong the life of your furnace and coax it into operating at maximum energy efficiency.

The following steps can help you learn how to clean a furnace and keep the unit in tip-top shape throughout the winter.

There are several reasons why it’s necessary for a homeowner to either know how to clean a gas furnace or know when to schedule a professional cleaning with an HVAC expert. However, the most important reason is that regular cleaning and maintenance help to extend the life of a furnace and HVAC system, while reducing the number of costly repairs and breakdowns.

Most system failures stem from dirt and dust choking out vital parts like the burners and flame sensors. Learning simple cleaning tasks, like how to clean a flame sensor on a furnace or how to clean the burners, prevents small complications from turning into expensive emergency repairs. Routine removal of soot, dirt, and dander as part of a furnace tune-up reduces wear and tear on internal components, helping the unit last its full 10- to 15-year expected lifespan.

If you still aren’t sure this is a necessary part of HVAC maintenance, check out this list of additional reasons for why it’s best to clean your furnace.

Most common furnace maintenance is not complicated—you just have to have a good vacuum cleaner and some basic tools and supplies. However, you do need to take a few precautions, so make sure to read and follow these steps in order to avoid skipping any important safety measures.

Recent findings suggest that always turn off the electrical power and fuel supply before you start any furnace project. You can turn off the electricity by either toggling the on-off switch on the unit or turning off the breaker in your breaker panel.

It has been revealed that in order to turn off the gas, locate the fuel shutoff valve. The location of the valve varies depending on whether you have an oil or a gas furnace. The valve should either be near the oil tank for an oil furnace or on the incoming gas pipe for a gas furnace. After you locate it, turn the valve off.

Wait several minutes to allow hot components to cool down before opening any panels. While you wait, use a microfiber cleaning cloth to wipe down the exterior of the furnace.

With a screwdriver, unscrew and remove the upper and lower service panels to gain access to the interior cavity of the furnace.

The Ridgid vac has a 7-foot heavy-duty locking hose and a 15-foot cord and made quick work of both wet and dry messes in our tests. Read the review.

Industry observers note that locate the small metal flame sensor rod near the burner assembly (often marked with a red or white connector). Unscrew and carefully pull the sensor out. Then gently scrub away soot or white-gray oxidation using fine-grit sandpaper or a wire brush until the metal shines. When you are done, wipe it clean and screw it back in.

Basic furnace filters are designed to trap dust, dirt, and airborne particulates before they can enter the furnace and potentially damage its components. As filters become full, they become unable to filter the air. While some filters can be cleaned, while others need to be replaced. During the heating season, clean or replace the furnace filter every 1 to 3 months.

Detach the burner cover and carefully slide or lift the burners out if they appear dirty or rusty. Brush any surface debris away with a soft-bristle brush or wash them in warm soapy water. After washing, rinse the burners thoroughly and dry them completely with compressed air before reinstalling.

According to recent reports, inspect the blower wheel fins for heavy dust buildup with a flashlight or your phone camera. If you see dust, use your vacuum to clean loose dust from the fins using a brush attachment. However, when the blower wheel is heavily caked in grime, it’s best to call a technician for a deep wash. It isn’t recommended for an inexperienced DIYer to remove the blower, so it’s best to stick to light vacuuming and dusting for this part of the process.

Put all access panels and doors back into place, ensuring any safety door switches are properly depressed, then turn the gas valve back on (parallel to the pipe) and restore power at the breaker or switch. Set your thermostat to Heat and watch to make sure the igniter glows, the gas catches smoothly into clean blue flames, and the blower kicks on.

Recent findings suggest that ideally, you should clean the furnace once a year to keep it in top condition before the fall heating season begins. It also is a good idea to perform a quick clean in the spring, vacuuming up any dust or soot. Proper care and maintenance will help prolong the life of your furnace, and keep it running at peak efficiency.

Strategy to replace or clean your furnace air filters every 1 to 3 months, clean the furnace about once a year in the spring, and hire a pro to inspect and deep clean it every fall. Also, consider having your home’s air ductwork cleaned every 3 to 5 years.

Sources indicate that although basic furnace maintenance can be handled by most homeowners, it makes sense to hire a professional for some tasks. For example, if you’ve noticed the furnace rumbling and can’t figure out why, then it’s best to call a pro for some on-site troubleshooting.

Additionally, there are some cleaning jobs that should be left to the experts, so instead of trying to figure out how to clean a furnace heat exchanger, remove a blower, or clean the coils, it’s better to book a deep furnace cleaning with a trained furnace technician. Save yourself some time and potential problems by calling an HVAC pro for any of the following issues.

Your furnace is a major investment in your home and your family’s comfort and safety. Regular cleaning and maintenance can save you money in the long run, because it will maximize the effective lifespan of your unit. Whether you are looking to maximize the efficiency and performance of a upcoming or existing unit, just a couple of hours of cleaning and maintenance every year will help keep your investment in tip-top shape and make sure your family stays comfy and cozy during the colder winter months.

Cleaning, changing filters, and lubricating your furnace are fairly simple steps in a process that really doesn’t take long. For a first-timer, it might take a few hours, since you might be dealing with unfamiliar equipment. After you have done it a few times, however, a full furnace clean should only take 1 to 2 hours. Changing the filters is even faster, and it only takes a few minutes to ensure that your air is clean and filtered.

Sources indicate that you should clean or service your furnace when you notice weak airflow, strange smells, or a spike in your energy bills. Here are other common signs that you should clean your furnace: • The furnace turns on and off rapidly when there are dirty flame sensors, clogged filters, or blocked burners that cause the unit to overheat.• Banging, screeching, or rattling sounds can mean the blower wheel is caked in debris or motor bearings need attention.• If dust settles rapidly around your furniture or return grilles soon after cleaning, your filter or blower compartment is likely overloaded.• The burner flame should burn steady and blue. A yellow flame means poor combustion and possible soot or carbon monoxide buildup.• An increase in sneezing, congestion, or dust-related irritation when the heat runs means the system is circulating allergens instead of trapping them.

Sources indicate that failing to clean your furnace can lead to carbon monoxide leaks, higher energy bills, and system breakdowns. Dirt and soot can cause incomplete combustion or crack the heat exchanger, releasing invisible, odorless, and deadly carbon monoxide gas into your home.Thick accumulations of dust, lint, and debris near the burners, wiring, or moving components can overheat and spark an electrical or mechanical fire. Also, a dirty filter or blocked flame sensor can cause the furnace to repeatedly turn on and off in short bursts, failing to heat your home evenly. Additionally, clogged air filters and dirty internal parts block airflow, forcing the system to work harder and consume more fuel or electricity to heat your space. Neglected filters stop trapping dust, pollen, pet hair, and allergens, which then circulate through your vents and trigger asthma or allergy symptoms. All of this added strain wears out the blower motor, flame sensor, and other mechanical parts much faster, significantly cutting down the typical 15- to 20-year lifespan of a furnace.

In a recent development, the average cost to clean a furnace ranges from about $70 to $400, depending on the type and location of your furnace. Typically, oil furnaces will cost more since they require deeper cleaning, and any units located in the attic or crawlspace will naturally cost more due to the difficulty accessing these areas.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • With autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months.
  • Shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.

With autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months. If you live in a snow-prone climate, this means getting out the shovels, salt and snowblower before the first flakes fly. Even if you’re not fresh to shoveling, it’s worth learning how to do it safely, as injuries can occur at any time.

Shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly. Ahead, learn expert-backed tips to shovel snow the right (and safe) way with insights from cardiologist Dr. Bradley Serwer.

In a recent development, the safest way to shovel snow is to push it as much as possible and avoid lifting. If you must lift snow to remove it, bend at the knees and lift with your legs instead of your back.

“The most important tool when preparing to shovel snow is good common sense,” Serwer indicates. “Dress appropriately and consider the risks of the job at hand.”.

Dress in layers that allow you to remove or open up a layer of clothing as you warm up to avoid getting overheated. Opt for a moisture wicking base layer, a mid-weight layer and a jacket that is wind-resistant and waterproof. Wear warm, waterproof gloves, a hat, warm socks and thick-soled winter boots. For particularly cold temperatures and high winds, add ski goggles and a balaclava to protect sensitive facial skin.

Consider a quick warm up and stretch session for a safer shoveling session. Get your blood pumping with some light activity like jumping jacks, walking in place or climbing up and down the stairs in your home. Gently stretch major muscle groups before heading outside.

It has been revealed that snow shovels are not all created equal. For safer shoveling, choose one that is less demanding on your back, joints and heart. Ergonomic shovels feature a curved handle that reduces back strain when lifting. Snow plow shovels are meant to push snow only, not lift it. And battery-powered shovels act like mini-snowblowers to quickly remove snow without any manual input.

It has been revealed that keep your back straight, bend at the knees and use your legs to lift snow for safer shoveling. Keep the loaded shovel close to your body, then, without twisting, turn your body toward the direction you place the snow. If snow is wet or deeper than six inches, remove it in smaller layers, rather than one heavy shovelful.

“It is often underestimated what kind of physical workload is required to shovel a substantial amount of snow,” Serwer claims. That’s why it’s important to pace yourself, stop regularly and blueprint ahead to avoid overexertion. Opt for a slow and steady pace, especially if you’re typically sedentary. Rigorous snow shoveling will swiftly lead to overexertion and cardiac strain. Going slow allows you to focus on safe shoveling technique, preventing possible muscle strains and pulls. Stay well-hydrated when shoveling and take regular breaks to allow your heart rate to return to normal and your muscles to recover.

Stop shoveling if you’re experiencing cardiac distress, cold-related conditions, dehydration or back strain.

“Shoveling snow can be a very strenuous activity, placing notable strain on the cardiovascular system,” Serwer claims. Know the signs of a heart attack before picking up a shovel, like chest pressure, shortness of breath, nausea and radiating arm pain. Stop immediately if you experience these symptoms and seek medical help. “Hire someone else to shovel, especially if you are at a high cardiac risk,” Serwer says.

In a recent development, dress in layers and cover exposed skin in freezing temperatures and wind. Even with these efforts, frostbite and hypothermia are real risks. Frostbite begins in extremities like fingers and toes, and exposed facial skin. Early signs include pale, cold skin and prickling or numb sensations. Hypothermia happens when core body temperatures drop too low and begins with clumsiness, foggy thinking, fatigue and intense shivering. Stop immediately and go inside to warm up if you experience these symptoms.

“It is very easy to become dehydrated while working in cold climates,” Serwer claims, as the human body suppresses the thirst response and dry winter air pulls additional moisture from our bodies. Notice signs of dehydration like fatigue, dry throat, cracked lips or a headache. “Dehydration is often overlooked, and people don’t replace the fluids as needed,” Serwer adds. Stop and take regular water breaks and continue drinking fluids for the remainder of the day if you notice these signs.

Shoveling puts strain on your spine and back, and can lead to serious, long term injuries like herniated disks, sciatica and lower back strains if you’re not careful. Beyond always lifting with your legs, stop shoveling if you feel the early signs of spine and back strain. These include a dull, aching in your lower back, sharp pain when bending or twisting, muscle cramping or shooting pains.

It is safer to push snow rather than lift it.

Recent findings suggest that individuals with heart disease, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure should not shovel snow. Those over 45 years old should also exercise caution.

We tested six air purifier and humidifier combinations for two months throughout a home, placing them in bedrooms, an office, a kitchen, and larger shared living areas. One model, the Blueair 2-in-1 Pro, had already been in long-term use for more than a year and was retested alongside the newer machines.

According to recent reports, we evaluated setup, controls and apps, humidification, purification response, noise, cleaning and refilling, and overall day-to-day usability. We also paid particular attention to automatic operation, noting how promptly each purifier responded when activities such as cooking or burning a candle changed surrounding air conditions. Since these are appliances many people leave visible and running continuously, design, reservoir access, maintenance, and how intrusive each unit felt during ordinary use also factored heavily into our scores and final awards.

Living with dry and unclean air can negatively affect comfort and health. Dry indoor air can cause an uncomfortable feeling at best and cracked skin at worst. Even “clean” indoor air can benefit from an air purifier, which can remove common pollutants such as pollen, pet hair, and smoke. Air purifying is even more key for allergy and asthma sufferers, who may notice a reduction in symptoms with a good air purifier.

There is a difference between air purifier and humidifier units: Purifiers remove pollutants from air, whereas humidifiers add moisture to the air. Combination units do both. Consider the following factors when shopping for the best air humidifier and purifier: room size, filtration system, reservoir capacity, and additional user-friendly features.

Sources indicate that air humidifier and purifier combo units are intended for use in one room. (Whole-house humidifier and air purifier options are separate products and are usually professionally installed into the home’s climate control system.) For optimal performance, a unit should most often be used in a room that is the size of the manufacturer’s recommendation.

It has been revealed that it’s possible to use a unit rated for a larger room in a smaller room, however, as long as a unit has a humidistat and auto-shutoff. The humidistat measures the ideal humidity, usually between 30 and 50 percent, and triggers the unit to shut off when ideal humidity is reached. Just know that if there’s no auto shut-off feature, a large humidifier can make a small room too humid.

While it’s crucial to take room size into account, the recommended room size can sometimes be misleading, so consider the CADR rating as well, explained ahead.

According to recent reports, air humidifiers and purifiers can have a few filter types, and many have a multistage filtration system. These systems can include activated carbon filters to remove odors, large particle filters, dust and pet hair filters, and the “gold standard,” HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filters. HEPA filters remove over 99.97 percent of dust mites, mold, pollen, bacteria, and other airborne particles measuring 0.3 microns (and actually trap smaller and larger particles even more effectively).

These extremely effective humidifiers with filters are shown to improve air quality. Shoppers who are interested in an air purifier and humidifier for allergies will want to look for a unit with a HEPA filter.

Air humidifiers and purifiers have a CADR (clean air delivery rate) score. This rating is used to measure an air purifier’s efficiency. It indicates the amount of filtered air a unit can deliver per minute and is often broken down into separate ratings for tobacco smoke, dust, and pollen. Products certified by the AHAM (Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers) are proven to live up to their CADR rating.

The higher the CADR score, the faster the filtration system. CADR is often used to calculate the appropriate square footage for a unit. The AHAM recommends that the CADR score of a unit should be a minimum of two-thirds of the room’s square footage.

Some units don’t display a CADR score and only display the room size the unit is suitable for. Knowing the CADR score is more reliable, as some manufacturers will recommend a room size that does not align with the AHAM’s recommendations. According to the AHAM, the recommended room size should be based on 4.8 air changes per hour (how many times the purifier cleans and circulates the air in a room). Many manufacturers will share a recommended room size based on only one or two air changes per hour to boost their square footage recommendation.

Air humidifier purifier units have a reservoir to hold water, which the machine turns into moisture to release into the air. The unit’s overall size (and therefore reservoir size) often corresponds to its suited room size. Small units are usually ideal for small or medium-size rooms, but they may need more frequent refilling if they also have a small reservoir tank. Larger units will need less frequent topping up, but they’ll also take up more space.

Keep in mind that usage habits will also affect how often the water tank needs refilling. Many air humidifiers and purifiers have a water tank between a half gallon and 1 gallon, but extra-large options are also available—we’ve included one with a 3-gallon-plus capacity on this list.

In our testing, reservoir design mattered almost as much as capacity. A slightly smaller tank that’s easy to remove, carry, and clean can be less frustrating than a larger reservoir with awkward access.

In a recent development, daily cleaning and maintenance can ensure that your air cleaner humidifier operates correctly and does not emit any harmful particles into a space. Users are encouraged to use distilled water in their humidifiers and purifiers to reduce general maintenance and germ buildup. Wash and dry the humidifier after each use to remove any potential bacteria, mold, minerals, and chemicals.

In a recent development, the Environmental Protection Agency advises using a 3 percent hydrogen peroxide solution to clean these machines every few days, clearing out any potential toxins. Finally, filters should be replaced as recommended by the manufacturer to ensure all contaminants are being removed.

Industry observers note that A good air humidifier and purifier should have a built-in humidistat that measures room humidity and adjusts operation accordingly. At minimum, the humidifier should shut off once the set humidity is reached to prevent the room from becoming overly damp.

Industry observers note that digital onboard controls are also useful, especially when they make it easy to adjust fan speed, humidity targets, and operating modes. Some models include a remote control for making changes from across the room.

Smart models can connect to Wi-Fi and a smartphone app for monitoring air quality, setting schedules, and changing settings remotely. In our testing, however, we often found the physical controls faster for everyday adjustments. Apps were most useful for checking air-quality data and receiving maintenance alerts.

Filter-change and refill reminders are particularly helpful, whether they appear in an app or through indicator lights on the unit itself.

Choosing the best air humidifier and purifier for your home really comes down to choosing a user-friendly option that’s suitable for the intended room size. Still wondering if a combined purifier and humidifier is the right choice? Read on for some frequently asked questions and answers on room air purifiers and humidifiers to narrow down the best option for your needs.

No, air purifiers do not dry out a space’s air supply, especially when the machine includes a humidifier. These machines are designed to improve indoor air quality by removing particles, microorganisms, and gases.

Industry observers note that no—air purifiers trap mold and common allergen particles in the air, but not the mold spores that may be present somewhere in the home. To completely get rid of a mold problem, consider an effective mold remover.

Yes. Air purifiers and humidifiers perform different functions, so they can be used at the same time without interfering with each other. An air purifier filters airborne pollutants, while a humidifier adds moisture to dry air. In fact, combination units like the ones we tested are specifically designed to perform both jobs from the same location. Just avoid over-humidifying the room; aim to keep indoor humidity between about 30 and 50 percent.

Industry observers note that yes. Air purifiers are designed to be left on at all times. In fact, running an air purifier as often as possible is the most effective way to improve air quality. After all, indoor air quality is always changing depending on the air quality outside and what you do inside, like cooking, cleaning, or smoking. Leaving the air purifier on will help improve air quality, regardless of exterior factors.

Industry observers note that in a way, yes. Stand-alone humidifiers don’t remove pollutants, but they do improve overall air quality by making the air feel more comfortable. Humidifiers can help keep indoor air humidity at an ideal level between 30 and 50 percent. Keeping indoor humidity in this sweet spot reduces the chance of mold growth and dust mites, which in turn can help maintain better air quality. To further improve air quality, look for a combined air purifier humidifier unit.

No, not necessarily. A humidifier is useful if you struggle with dry indoor air. It’s not necessary (and can even be detrimental) to run a humidifier in humid homes. If the air in your home often dips beneath 30 percent, consider using a humidifier.

The unit needs to run for a certain length of time for you to take full advantage of the air purifier and humidifier benefits. Effectiveness depends on a wide range of factors, including the room size, the air purifier’s filtration system, the unit’s settings, and the surrounding humidity level. Consider the CADR rating and recommended room size to find a suitable unit. When these metrics are all taken into account, a good air purifier should create cleaner air in around just 15 minutes.

  • Drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in.
  • Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Sources indicate that those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks. Here’s what inspectors check and what happens when a truck pulls into a weigh station.

Drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in. Once a semitruck exits and rejoins the highway, it’s hard to tell what goes on in between.

Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.

Sources indicate that truck weigh stations help states enforce weight limits and spot safety problems. Trucks can weigh too much overall or carry too much weight on certain axles, putting extra strain on roads and bridges. On the Interstate System, the standard federal limits are 80,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, 20,000 pounds on a single axle, and 34,000 pounds on a tandem axle. Federal bridge weight rules and certain exceptions can also affect how much a truck may legally carry. Limits on other roads can vary.

Sources indicate that rules vary by state. “Some require all commercial motor vehicles to stop, while others require only those above a certain weight to stop,” according to the Federal Highway Administration. “Ultimately, States must certify that they are enforcing their weight limits on certain highways in order not to jeopardize their receipt of Federal highway funds.”.

Sources indicate that drivers who pull in follow signs directing them to a scale, where their trucks are weighed either while moving slowly or at a complete stop. If the weight is within the limits, they may be cleared to leave. Inspectors may still pull a truck aside for a closer look even when its weight is fine, based on screening results, visible defects, or random selection. An overweight truck may also be inspected further.

Inspectors may check a truck’s tires, brakes, lights, and cargo, along with the driver’s records. They may also review credentials and permits, such as registration and fuel-tax paperwork, along with the driver’s hours-of-service logs. “There are eight levels of inspections ranging from the Level I Inspection, which evaluates both the driver and vehicle, to inspection levels with a more specific area of focus, such as Level VI for radioactive materials and Level VIII for electronic inspections,” according to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance.

It has been revealed that drivers of overweight trucks may receive a citation or have to move or remove some cargo before leaving. The exact consequences vary by state and violation.

Sources indicate that more serious safety problems, like faulty brakes, can put a truck or driver out of service. A truck placed out of service can’t return to the road until the problem is fixed. Drivers placed out of service must wait until their restrictions end.

Some trucks can skip the stop altogether through electronic bypass programs. These programs use safety records and other information to determine whether a driver can continue without entering the station. Drivers still have to follow any signs or signals telling them to stop.

    It has been revealed that how high you should mount a TV on the wall is a question that stumps binge-watchers and cinephiles alike. Position the TV too high or low, and you’ll have to crane your neck or slump your shoulders to take in the on-screen action. A misplaced TV can also be a pain to remove and reinstall at another height, which is why it’s in your best interest to get it right the first time.

    Sources indicate that manufacturers and home entertainment enthusiasts recommend mounting a TV at eye level for optimal viewing, but the best TV height for you also depends on TV wall mount type, screen size, and other factors. The answer to how high should a TV be mounted sometimes varies slightly for those reasons, but these rules of thumb will help you come to the right decision.

    According to recent reports, as you think about how high to mount a TV, most experts use the center of the TV screen as the main point of reference, no matter the screen size. Unless you’re mounting a TV for just one person to use, keeping the center of the TV at a comfortable viewing height for most people should be the goal. Forty-two inches from the floor to the center of the screen is the ideal TV mount height under most circumstances.

    Recent findings suggest that for tailored comfort, however, you can actually factor your height, and the height of fellow household members, into your TV’s height from the floor. You’ll find a more exact center point for your TV mount by measuring the distance from the floor to each household member’s eye level when sitting. Add those measurements together and divide by the total number of people for your bespoke TV wall mount height.

    In a recent development, note that while TV size doesn’t always affect mounting height, a TV’s dimensions matter when considering optimal viewing distance. If you have a large, 65-inch or 75-inch TV, it may be uncomfortable to watch if your seating is too close to the wall it’s mounted on, regardless of how high or low it’s mounted. In these and similar cases, use a TV mount height calculator to simplify the math and guesswork involved in determining the best TV viewing distance and height for your space.

    Recent findings suggest that these LED strip lights connect to your TV’s USB port to light up your screen from behind. See our full review.

    Not all of the seats in a living room are going to be the same height. An open floor plan with counter-height bar stools, bar-height stools, and a sofa, for example, can complicate TV mounting height. Counter-height bar stools are higher off of the floor than sofa seats—anywhere from 24 to 29 inches to reach the counter. Bar-height stools are even taller, at 29 to 33 inches.

    If the seats in a room are at various heights, or the room in question isn’t a living room, consider the following approaches.

    There are several other spatial and functional considerations to account for when determining the position and height of a wall-mounted TV. In your home, these may include:.

    When thinking about how high to hang a TV, you shouldn’t position it so high that viewers need to tilt their heads up more than 35 degrees from eye level in order to see the top of the screen, according to the Society of Motion Picture & Television Engineers.

    Sources indicate that tilting a TV’s screen downward is one way to position it higher than eye level without causing discomfort or neck strain, if necessary. This requires upgrading from a basic low-profile mount (which is stationary) to one of two other types of TV mounts: a tilting wall mount (which can move up or down) or full-motion mount (which can swivel in all directions). For a full walkthrough of how to install either type of mount, check out our guide on how to mount a TV to the wall.

Knowing how high to mount your TV depends on a few factors, and keeping the center of the screen at eye level is the most critical. While professional TV mount installation is always an option, careful measurements and the above tips will get your TV properly positioned for a comfortable premiere.

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    GTA6 let's you take a break from a life of crime to make some much-needed home repairs on Jason and Lucia's house.

    Just in case your algorithm is different from mine, here’s some news: Grand Theft Auto 6 officially released today. After 13 years of waiting, fans of the open-world action-adventure video game series can finally dive into a new, richly detailed and fully realized virtual world. Boot up the game, and you’ll find yourself faced with surprising realism, a world of crime, and the ability to do just about whatever you want. That’s right, even… DIY home improvement jobs?

    Sources indicate that yep, you’re reading that right. As part of its commitment to realism, GTA developer Rockstar Games has given players the ability to do some honest-to-goodness, roll-up-your-sleeves-and-get-to-work home improvement virtually.

    Industry observers note that and it’s not just a short cutscene where you see the house magically go from disrepair to fully fixed up. You, as the player, have to actually do the work, whether you’re drywalling, painting, or roofing. Luckily, it’s just a video game because the game is also set in a fictional version of Florida in the summer, which is probably one of the last places on earth you’d want to be stuck doing any sort of construction work.

    Let’s take a look at a few of the home improvement jobs done by GTA6‘s Jason Duval and see if his work meets Family Handyman’s standards.

    With his lady friend Lucia on the way back from prison, Jason decides to fix up the place… including the unfinished framing in the center of his living room. Luckily, Jason knows how to hang drywall. The gameplay represents the job pretty accurately— Jason holds the drywall in place and screws it into the studs with an impact driver. We don’t get to see any taping or mudding, though. 7/10.

    In a recent development, next, we’ll inspect whether Jason should perhaps prioritize a career as a painter over his life of crime. The painting section is also pretty accurate to the average DIY painting experience. Jason has to choose between three different color options before pouring the paint into a tray and using a roller to paint the wall. It’s pretty boring, which is honestly just like painting in real life — so bonus points for immersive realism. 8/10.

    One of the first things Jason knows he has to fix before Lucia arrives is the massive hole in his roof that’s letting in a near-constant drip of rain. Luckily, like a lot of DIYers, he has some roofing experience, a cordless nail gun and a stack of shingles just lying around for some reason. Again, this section is pretty realistic. If gamers want the full Florida roofing experience, though, they’ll have to crank their heaters to maximum or perhaps play the game in a sauna. 6/10.

    Look, I get it. The Grand Theft Auto series is about living out fantasies, providing gamers a sandbox where they can virtually experience the impossible.

    But still… “House repairs complete” is a bridge too far. Ask any DIYer, and they will tell you no house is ever fully repaired. Pretending home improvement work could ever be finished is just not realistic and really took me out of the experience. 3/10.

    According to recent reports, overall, the game is cool. But to be honest, I’m not sure what the point is now that the house repairs are complete.

When you’re revamping your kitchen lighting design, it’s smart to assess everything from function and fixture to the type of light bulbs you use. This is suitable for countertops made of butcher block, stone, or another material with a flat or matte finish. But with marble, granite, or similarly glossy materials, the center of the beam can produce a distracting glare even when placed a few feet away from it. To avoid this, place LED light strips inside light housings, which are aluminum channels with frosted covers that help diffuse bright light and minimize glare on shiny kitchen surfaces.

    Industry observers note that incandescent, compact fluorescent light (CFL), and LED light bulbs for the kitchen come in one of three color temperatures that describe the color characteristics of the light the bulb emits. There’s Soft White (2700K to 3000 Kelvins (K)), Cool White/Bright White (3500K to 4100K), and Daylight (5000K to 6500K). The higher the bulb temperature, the cooler (i.e., bluer) the light it emits; the lower the temperature, the warmer (i.e., more amber) the light. Choose the color temperature best suited for the function of the fixture:.

    Industry observers note that the order was issued by a Mississippi state court Oct. 12; the case has just been removed to federal court, which will now consider the defendant's arguments against the injunction. Here's the key passage from the injunction, a temporary restraining order that was issued before the defendant could respond:.

    Here's the heart of plaintiffs' argument:.

    Defendants argue that the order isn't authorized by the Mississippi's Protection from Domestic Abuse Law or by the Mississippi rules governing ordinary temporary restraining orders. But it also argues (I think correctly) that is an overbroad prior restraint that violates the First Amendment:.

    In a recent development, the order does not merely prohibit threats or harassment. It prohibits speech about the Plaintiffs, their families, and their lawyers—whether truthful or false, threatening or harmless, harassing or not. And it does so before that speech occurs. The Supreme Court has repeatedly condemned such prior restraints, particularly when imposed without notice or an opportunity to be heard.

    The Court need not decide whether Mr. Hughes's commentary was fair, tasteful, or justified. The question is whether the law permits this order. It does not. The order should be dissolved, and the motion for a preliminary injunction denied….

    A judicial order "forbidding certain communications when issued in advance of the time that such communications are to occur" is a prior restraint…. "Any system of prior restraints on communication bears a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity." Such restraints are unconstitutional "except in exceptional circumstances." .As the Supreme Court held in Organization for a Better Austin v. Keefe (1971), {the party seeking to suppress speech} "carries a heavy burden of showing justification for the imposition of such a restraint." ….

    The remedy for false or injurious statements lies in "actions under libel laws providing for redress and punishment, and not in proceedings to restrain the publication." [But t]he October 12 Order … does not impose consequences for particular statements adjudicated unlawful. It prohibits Mr. Hughes from speaking about entire categories of people in the future. That is a prior restraint in its most direct form which is presumed unconstitutional….

    Test Masters Educ. Servs., Inc. v. Singh (5th Cir. 2005) … recognized that a court may enjoin "harassing communication" and "repeated invasions of privacy." But an injunction prohibiting all communication, rather than limiting itself to "threatening or harassing conduct," "swept too broadly" and constituted an unconstitutional restraint. Id.….

    Recent findings suggest that plaintiffs cannot justify the restraint merely by characterizing Mr. Hughes's commentary as malicious, coercive, or injurious. The Supreme Court rejected that reasoning in Keefe. There, the Court held that an individual's "interest in being free from public criticism of his business practices" did not justify an injunction against speech…. Plaintiffs may have remedies for unlawful conduct. But those remedies do not include an order forbidding Mr. Hughes from speaking about them at all….

    Defendant also argues (again correctly, I think) that the order was unconstitutional because defendant wasn't given an opportunity to be heard before the order was entered:.

    The absence of notice presents a separate constitutional defect. In Carroll v. President & Commissioners of Princess Anne (1968), the Supreme Court set aside a short ex parte order restraining expression because of "a basic infirmity in the procedure by which it was obtained." The order "was issued ex parte, without notice to petitioners and without any effort, however informal, to invite or permit their participation in the proceedings.".

    There is a place in our jurisprudence for ex parte issuance, without notice, of temporary restraining orders of short duration; There is no place within the area of basic freedoms guaranteed by the First Amendment for such orders where no showing is made that it is impossible to serve or to notify the opposing parties and to give them an opportunity to participate.

    Industry observers note that the Court also rejected the suggestion that a later hearing could cure the problem. The availability of a subsequent opportunity to be heard "does not overcome the infirmity in the absence of a showing of justification for the ex parte nature of the proceedings.".

    It has been revealed that the reason is straightforward. "The value of judicial decision-making … is substantially diluted where the process is ex parte, because the Court does not have available the fundamental instrument for judicial judgment: "an adversary proceeding in which both parties may participate." And where First Amendment freedoms are at stake, any order must be "couched in the narrowest terms that will accomplish the pin-pointed objective.".

    The October 12 Order fails both principles. It was entered without notice or an adversary hearing. It contains no finding that notifying Mr. Hughes was impossible. And far from identifying a narrow category of unlawful speech, it prohibits virtually any online commentary concerning the Plaintiffs, their families, or their counsel.

    It has been revealed that carroll is directly controlling on the constitutional defect. An ex parte order restraining expression cannot stand without a showing that notice and participation were impossible. No such showing appears here….

    It has been revealed that during a power outage, a generator that runs on gasoline can provide enough juice to keep your lights on, your groceries from spoiling, and your fans spinning. Set up a portable unit outside your home, and connect appliances inside to its numerous outlets via extension cords.     While a portable generator might cost several hundred or even thousands of dollars depending on size and model, when compared to a standby generator, which would kick on automatically to power your home, it’s certainly less expensive. Plus, you may not need a professional electrician to install a portable generator, and you can easily take the unit with you should you move. All that mentioned, proper operation of the machine is crucial to ensure the safety of your family and your community.

    Before you start up a portable generator, bear in mind these two essential considerations:.

    WEN’s 5600-watt generator has a push-button start and is powerful enough to run household essentials; noise level is about 88 dB. Read the review.

    Because portable gas generators emit carbon monoxide while they’re running and for some time afterward, positioning the generator properly and practicing careful carbon monoxide safety is critical.

    In a recent development, before you start up the generator, check the fuel gauge and fill the tank with gasoline as needed. (Make sure the generator is on a level surface to get an accurate reading on the fuel gauge.) If you need to add fuel, consult the owner’s manual for fuel requirements.

    In a recent development, next, check the oil level, which is like checking the oil in your car. Locate the oil dipstick (often below a removable maintenance panel). Pull out the dipstick, wipe it off, and then re-insert it. Carefully pull the dipstick straight out once more, then look to see if the oil on the stick falls between the lower and upper limit marks imprinted on the dipstick. Add or change the oil if necessary, referring to your owner’s manual for how to add, what kind to use, and how frequently it needs to be changed.

    Sources indicate that before plugging in, ensure that you won’t overload the generator by connecting more appliances and lights than it is rated to handle. Add up the starting and running wattage of the appliances you want to power simultaneously; refer to their respective user manuals or check the backs or sides of the machines to find this information. The total number should not exceed the wattage limitations of your generator. Check your user’s manual if you’re unsure of how many watts of power your generator can handle. Stagger the use of appliances if necessary to prevent overloading the generator.

    Follow your user manual for instructions on turning on the machine. You typically will need to turn the circuit breaker off and turn the fuel valve on before starting it up. Give the machine a few minutes to warm up, then flip the circuit breaker on.

    Use long, heavy-duty extension cords made for outdoor use to connect appliances to the generator one by one so as not to overload it. Examine cords before use to ensure they are in good condition with no rips or tears. The cord’s wattage rating should be greater than the wattage of what you’ve plugged into it.

    It has been revealed that to shut down the generator, turn off or disconnect the appliances plugged into it. Then refer to your user’s manual to power down the generator—typically you’ll need to turn the circuit breaker, engine switch, and fuel valve to the “off” position.

    Wait until the generator is completely cooled down before storing it once power is restored. If you don’t anticipate needing it again for more than a month, drain the fuel and carburetor. Leaving old fuel can damage the generator’s internal parts. Refer to your owner’s manual for storage instructions.

    When running a portable generator, safety is the name of the game. Keep these tips in mind before, during, and after use.

    Particulate matter—including tiny airborne particles like pollen, smoke, soot, and other debris—is one of the most common indoor air pollutants, says Dr. Jaspreet Dhau, an expert on indoor air quality and purification and vice president of research and development at Molekule in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. “Fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, which is a particle measuring 2.5 microns [micrometers] or smaller, is a concern because it can travel deep into the respiratory system,” says Dhau. Common sources include cooking, burning candles, using a fireplace, vacuuming, and even opening windows when outdoor pollution levels are high.

    It has been revealed that VOCs are gases released by certain household products and materials such as paint, solvents, flooring, furniture, adhesives, cleaning supplies, air fresheners, and personal care products. “VOC levels may be higher during and after a home renovation, when upcoming furniture is brought into a home, or when products containing chemical ingredients are used without adequate ventilation,” indicates Dhau. For example, certain pressed wood furniture and building materials can release formaldehyde, he explains.

    Industry observers note that carbon monoxide (CO) is a combustion byproduct, a pollutant released when something burns. “In a typical home, sources can include gas stoves, fireplaces, wood-burning stoves, furnaces, water heaters, candles, and tobacco products,” says Dhau. “Carbon monoxide is especially dangerous because it’s colorless and odorless, making it difficult to detect without a working CO alarm.”.

    It has been revealed that biological contaminants such as dust mites and pet dander are airborne pollutants that originate from living organisms, indicates Dhau. “Dust mites are a frequent matter and tend to collect in mattresses, carpets, upholstered furniture, and bedding. They can enter homes through open windows, pets, clothing, and HVAC systems,” he explains. Signs you might have a problem include frequent dust buildup on surfaces, allergy symptoms, excess pet hair and dander, and dust accumulating around air vents, adds Bill Myers, indoor air quality expert and group manager for technical sales at Panasonic Eco Systems North America.

    Quiet, effective and easy to use, this commercial-grade unit cleans the air with a washable pre-filter, a carbon filter, and a HEPA filter.

    Sources indicate that this short new article of mine has now been published in the Notre Dame Law Review. The Introduction:.

    Sources indicate that there are many vital major-picture questions about original meaning and the Free Speech, Free Press, Assembly, and Petition Clauses. This short Essay will leave those questions for others. Instead, it will offer as illustrations some specific, concrete questions—and, in some instances, answers—about original meaning and the freedom of expression. I hope these narrow illustrations can help us think about the broader questions.

    From the table of contents, which should illustrate the subjects I cover:.

    I. Broad Evidence, and Silently Consistent Precedents A. "The Liberty of the Press Is Not Confined to Newspapers and Periodicals" B. Symbolic Expression C. Civil Liability II. Scant Evidence: Provoking a Riot III. Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels.

    Whether courts should shift the constitutional law of free expression to a more originalist footing is an important and difficult question. Perhaps it's a question that should be resolved entirely as a matter of constitutional theory—maybe such an approach is required by proper interpretive principles, or maybe it's forbidden by other principles (for instance, having to do with precedent).

    But it's also possible that the answer may rest in part on how practically usable an originalist framework is likely to be. And to consider that, it's helpful to have in mind some practical questions. Some are already familiar, for instance questions related to damages liability in libel cases, obscenity law, and the like. This short Essay has aimed to help supplement those familiar examples with some others that haven't been much discussed; I hope others who think about the topic can find them useful.

    I expect I'll post excerpts from the article in the coming days.
